title: Basic Operation
question: How does it work?

operating_sequence: Initial startup bias: R1 (10K) and R4 (10K) provide small base currents to Q1 and Q2 respectively through voltage dividers with R2 (18K) and R5 (18K) from PrimaryBT1 (6V)

Magnetic field build-up: When either transistor begins conducting, collector current flows through its respective T1 primary winding, creating increasing magnetic flux in the trifilar transformer core

Regenerative feedback: Changing magnetic flux induces voltage in T1 trigger winding (T1 pin 3), which couples through potentiometer R7 (1K) and resistors R3/R6 (560R) to transistor bases, providing positive feedback

Transistor saturation: Positive feedback rapidly increases base drive, causing transistor to enter saturation with full collector current limited primarily by winding resistance and saturation voltage

Magnetic saturation and cutoff: As magnetic core approaches saturation, flux rate-of-change decreases, reducing trigger winding voltage below level needed to sustain base current, causing transistor turn-off

Flyback energy transfer: Collapsing magnetic field generates high-voltage flyback pulse across primary windings; D1 rectifies Q1 channel flyback to ChargeBT2 positive terminal; D2 provides path between ChargeBT2+ and ChargeBT1+ for Q2 channel energy
determinations.startup_behavior: Circuit relies on base bias resistor networks (R1-R2 for Q1, R4-R5 for Q2) to provide initial turn-on current when PrimaryBT1 is connected. Voltage divider action creates approximately 2.6V at each base (6V * 18K / (10K + 18K)), providing sufficient bias to initiate small collector current through T1 primary windings. Any noise, component asymmetry, or initial magnetic state will cause one channel to begin oscillating first, though both channels can sustain independent oscillation once started.
determinations.switching_mechanism: Magnetically-coupled regenerative feedback through T1 trifilar transformer trigger winding. Increasing collector current produces increasing magnetic flux (dΦ/dt), which induces voltage V = N * dΦ/dt in trigger winding. This voltage adds to base bias current, creating positive feedback loop that drives transistor from cutoff through active region to saturation in microseconds. Switching is self-timed by magnetic core properties and winding inductance rather than external clock or RC timing network.
determinations.oscillation_cycle: Each channel operates as independent blocking oscillator: (1) Base bias initiates small collector current, (2) Magnetic flux increases in T1 core, (3) Trigger winding voltage provides regenerative base drive, (4) Transistor saturates with maximum collector current, (5) Core approaches saturation where dΦ/dt decreases, (6) Trigger voltage falls below threshold, (7) Transistor turns off abruptly, (8) Magnetic field collapses generating flyback pulse, (9) Flyback energy transfers through diode to charging batteries, (10) Magnetic field dissipates completely, (11) Base bias resistor re-initiates next cycle. Typical blocking oscillator frequency range 1-50 kHz depending on core material, winding inductance, and supply voltage.
determinations.control_mechanism: Potentiometer R7 (1K) adjusts coupling strength between T1 trigger winding and transistor bases. Moving wiper toward R3/R6 junction increases trigger winding signal to bases, potentially increasing oscillation frequency and altering duty cycle. Moving wiper toward T1 pin 3 reduces feedback strength, potentially lowering frequency or causing one channel to dominate. R7 provides tuning control over relative phase relationship between Q1 and Q2 oscillations, enabling adjustment from synchronized operation to independent asynchronous oscillation of the two channels.

title: Energy Flow
question: Where does the energy go?

determinations.energy_source: PrimaryBT1 (6V DC) provides electrical energy through voltage divider networks R1-R2 and R4-R5 to bias transistor bases, and through transistor collectors to T1 primary windings where it stores as magnetic field energy during conduction phase.

storage_elements.element: T1 primary windings (pins 1-2 for Q1 channel, pins 4-6 for Q2 channel)
storage_elements.role: Magnetic field energy storage during transistor saturation; energy accumulates as ½LI² where L is primary inductance and I is collector current ramping up linearly
Electrochemical energy storage receiving flyback pulse energy through D1 and D2 rectification; accumulates transferred magnetic energy as battery charge

storage_elements.element: Transistor base-emitter junctions Q1 and Q2
storage_elements.role: Temporary charge storage during positive feedback drive from T1 trigger winding (pin 3); capacitance negligible compared to magnetic storage

determinations.transfer_path: Primary battery → transistor base bias networks → trigger winding regenerative feedback → saturated transistor collector current → magnetic field buildup in T1 core → abrupt cutoff → collapsing magnetic field induces high voltage across primary windings → flyback pulse rectified by D1 (Q1 channel to ChargeBT2+) and D2 (cross-coupling between ChargeBT2+ and ChargeBT1+) → charging current flows into series battery configuration → electrochemical energy storage in ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2.

losses.estimate: V_CE(sat) × I_C × duty_cycle, typically 0.5-2W per transistor at estimated 1-2A collector current with 0.3-0.5V saturation voltage and 20-40% duty cycle

losses.mechanism: Core hysteresis and eddy current loss
losses.estimate: Proportional to frequency and flux density squared; unknown without core material specification but typical ferrite cores at kHz range show 0.1-0.5W loss

title: Physical Principles
question: Why does it behave this way?

determinations.magnetic_behavior: T1 trifilar transformer core operates via Ampère's law: collector current I_C through primary windings (pins 1-2 for Q1, pins 4-6 for Q2) generates magnetomotive force F = N*I establishing magnetic flux Φ in ferromagnetic core. Faraday's law governs regenerative feedback: time-varying flux dΦ/dt induces voltage V_trigger = N_trigger * dΦ/dt on trigger winding (pin 3), providing positive base drive that accelerates transistor saturation. Core B-H curve nonlinearity causes flux rate-of-change to decrease as core approaches saturation (B → B_sat), reducing trigger voltage below threshold needed to sustain base current, initiating abrupt transistor cutoff. During cutoff, stored magnetic energy E_mag = ½LI² releases as collapsing flux generates high-voltage flyback pulse V_flyback ≈ L(dI/dt) across primary windings, with amplitude limited by charging battery clamping voltage plus diode forward drop.
determinations.electric_field_interactions: Electric field energy storage occurs primarily in transistor base-emitter depletion capacitance C_BE and collector-base junction capacitance C_CB during switching transitions, with stored energy E_cap = ½CV² being negligible (<1 μJ) compared to magnetic storage (>1 mJ typical). Voltage divider networks R1-R2 and R4-R5 establish electric field across base-emitter junctions via Ohm's law V_BE = I_bias * R1 where I_bias = 6V/(10kΩ + 18kΩ) ≈ 0.21 mA provides initial forward bias. Flyback pulse creates transient electric field stress across diode D1/D2 reverse-biased junctions and transistor collector-emitter off-state, with peak voltage determined by magnetic energy release clamped by charging battery impedance. Potentiometer R7 wiper position modulates electric field distribution in trigger winding coupling network, controlling voltage division between trigger winding output and transistor base nodes.
determinations.semiconductor_physics: BD243C NPN bipolar junction transistors operate via minority carrier injection physics: forward-biased base-emitter junction (V_BE ≥ 0.7V from trigger winding drive) injects electrons from emitter into base region, diffusing to reverse-biased collector junction where electric field sweeps carriers to collector terminal, producing amplified collector current I_C = β*I_B (β ≈ 50-150 typical for BD243C). During saturation phase, both junctions forward-biased with excess base current storing minority carriers in base region and collector depletion layer (charge storage time τ_s ≈ 1-5 μs). Transistor cutoff occurs when trigger voltage falls below V_BE threshold, halting carrier injection; stored base charge must recombine before collector current ceases, creating finite storage delay that limits turn-off speed. Flyback voltage stress must remain below V_CEO breakdown (≈100V for BD243C per datasheet) to prevent avalanche multiplication and destructive failure. 1N4007 diodes rectify via PN junction physics: forward bias (anode positive during flyback) allows majority carrier drift conduction with ~0.7-1.0V drop; reverse bias (blocking when transistor conducts) supports depletion region electric field up to 1000V peak reverse voltage rating.

governing_equations.name: Faraday's Law of Induction
governing_equations.applicability: Voltage induced in T1 trigger winding (N_trigger turns) by time-varying magnetic flux Φ(t) in core; negative sign indicates Lenz's law opposition to flux change; governs regenerative feedback mechanism driving transistor bases

governing_equations.applicability: Magnetomotive force F produced by N turns carrying current I creates magnetic field intensity H in core; relates collector current to magnetic flux density B = μ*H where μ is core permeability; determines energy storage rate during transistor conduction

governing_equations.name: Magnetic Energy Storage
governing_equations.applicability: Energy stored in magnetic field of T1 primary winding inductance L when carrying peak collector current I; released as flyback pulse during transistor cutoff; determines available energy for charging battery transfer

simulation_hooks.description: Capture flyback voltage V_flyback(t) across primary winding and calculate dI/dt during transistor turn-off from measured current decay, verify V = L*dI/dt relationship using known or extracted inductance L
simulation_hooks.validates: Flyback voltage generation by Faraday's law; inductive voltage spike equation V = L*dI/dt during rapid current collapse
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: Peak flyback voltage 30-100V with dI/dt = 10⁶-10⁷ A/s (1-3A collapse in 0.1-1 μs turn-off time); voltage spike amplitude V_peak = L*dI/dt matches prediction within 20% accounting for parasitic capacitance damping

simulation_hooks.description: Measure base-emitter voltage V_BE(t) during regenerative feedback transition showing exponential relationship I_C = I_S*exp(V_BE/V_T) as positive feedback drives transistor from cutoff (V_BE < 0.5V) through active region (0.6-0.7V) to saturation (V_BE > 0.7V)
simulation_hooks.validates: Semiconductor physics: BJT exponential transconductance and current gain β = ∂I_C/∂I_B govern regenerative feedback speed and saturation characteristics
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: V_BE rises from ~0.2V (bias network alone) to 0.7-0.9V (saturated with trigger winding drive) in microseconds; collector current increases exponentially then linearly as transistor enters saturation with both junctions forward-biased

simulation_hooks.description: FFT analysis of collector current waveform identifying fundamental frequency f₀ and harmonic content; compare core loss calculation P_core = k*f^n*B_max^m (Steinmetz equation) using measured frequency and estimated flux density to total circuit losses
simulation_hooks.validates: Magnetic core loss mechanisms (hysteresis ∝ f, eddy currents ∝ f²) contribute to energy dissipation proportional to operating frequency and flux swing amplitude
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: Fundamental frequency 1-50 kHz with significant odd harmonics (3f₀, 5f₀) from rectangular switching waveform; core losses 0.1-0.5W estimated from Steinmetz equation comparable to measured total loss budget minus resistive and semiconductor losses

title: Component Roles
question: What does every component contribute?

components.purpose: Primary energy source providing DC voltage to both oscillator channels via voltage divider bias networks and transistor collectors; supplies power for magnetic field buildup in T1 during conduction phases
interactions: Negative terminal connects to Q1 emitter (Net-_PrimaryBT1--_) and Q2 emitter providing common ground reference
Positive terminal connects through ChargeBT1 to common rail (Net-_ChargeBT1--_) forming series battery configuration
Sources bias current through R1-R2 divider to Q1 base and R4-R5 divider to Q2 base for startup
Delivers collector current through saturated transistors to T1 primary windings during conduction
components.design_intent: 6V nominal voltage chosen to provide sufficient base-emitter bias (>0.7V) through voltage dividers while limiting peak collector current and magnetic saturation time in T1; series connection with ChargeBT1 enables energy extraction from primary battery while charging separate battery bank

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower voltage (<4V) may fail to sustain oscillation through voltage divider losses; higher voltage (>12V) increases collector current, flyback voltage stress on transistors/diodes, and power dissipation requiring heatsinking

components.purpose: Charging battery accepting flyback energy from both oscillator channels; forms series configuration with ChargeBT2 creating 12V nominal charging rail; acts as intermediate node between primary battery and charging batteries
interactions: Positive terminal (Net-_ChargeBT1-+_) connects to D2 cathode receiving cross-coupled energy from Q2 channel
Negative terminal (Net-_ChargeBT1--_) connects to PrimaryBT1 positive, ChargeBT2 negative, and T1 pins 1/5 creating common rail
Series with ChargeBT2 presents ~12V clamping voltage to flyback pulses through D1/D2 rectification
Accepts pulsed charging current during magnetic energy release from T1 core collapse
components.design_intent: Series battery configuration doubles charging voltage compared to single 6V battery, reducing peak current stress during flyback pulses while enabling higher energy transfer per cycle; supports Bedini SSG design principle of using separate charging battery bank from primary source

possible_substitutions.part: 6-12V rechargeable battery (lead-acid, NiMH, Li-ion with protection)
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Higher voltage batteries reduce charging current peak but require proportionally higher flyback voltage generation; battery chemistry affects charging efficiency and acceptable pulse charging characteristics

components.purpose: Second charging battery in series with ChargeBT1; primary recipient of Q1 channel flyback energy through D1; positive terminal serves as cross-coupling node for D2 connection to ChargeBT1
interactions: Positive terminal (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_) connects to D1 cathode, D2 anode, T1 pin 6, Q2 collector, and R5 forming critical distribution node
Negative terminal connects to ChargeBT1 negative at common rail (Net-_ChargeBT1--_)
Series combination with ChargeBT1 provides ~12V charging rail voltage referenced to primary battery ground
Receives direct flyback pulse energy from Q1 channel via D1 rectification
components.design_intent: Upper battery in series charging configuration receives majority of Q1 channel energy while positive terminal node enables D2 cross-coupling for Q2 channel energy distribution; dual-battery series arrangement characteristic of Bedini SSG designs for voltage multiplication

possible_substitutions.part: 6-12V rechargeable battery matching ChargeBT1 chemistry and capacity
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Mismatched battery capacities or chemistries cause unequal charging rates and potential overcharge/undercharge; voltage mismatch affects flyback pulse clamping and energy distribution

components.purpose: Primary switching transistor for channel 1; controls magnetizing current through T1 pins 1-2 winding; operates in saturation during conduction and cutoff during flyback; regenerative feedback from trigger winding drives base
interactions: Collector (Net-_D1-A_) connects to T1 pin 2 and D1 anode forming primary winding current path and flyback voltage node
Base (Net-_Q1-B_) receives bias from R1-R2 divider and regenerative drive from trigger winding via R3-R7 network
Emitter connects to primary battery negative (Net-_PrimaryBT1--_) providing ground reference
Saturates when trigger winding voltage exceeds ~0.7V threshold, conducting 0.5-3A collector current through T1 primary
Cutoff when magnetic core approaches saturation reducing trigger voltage below base threshold
components.design_intent: BD243C NPN power transistor selected for sufficient current gain (β≈50-150), collector current rating (6A continuous), and voltage rating (V_CEO≥100V) to handle flyback spikes; TO-220 package enables heatsinking for 1-2W typical conduction loss

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower current gain requires stronger base drive from trigger winding; higher V_CE(sat) increases conduction loss; faster switching speed (lower storage time) improves efficiency but may require snubbing for voltage spike protection

components.purpose: Primary switching transistor for channel 2; controls magnetizing current through T1 pins 4-6 winding; operates identically to Q1 but with independent base drive enabling dual-channel oscillation with adjustable phase relationship
interactions: Collector (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_) connects to T1 pin 6 forming secondary primary winding current path; shares node with D1 cathode, D2 anode, and ChargeBT2 positive
Base (Net-_Q2-B_) receives bias from R4-R5 divider and regenerative drive from trigger winding via R6-R7 network
Emitter connects to primary battery negative (Net-_PrimaryBT1--_) parallel with Q1 emitter
Operates in saturation-cutoff cycle governed by magnetic feedback similar to Q1 but potentially phase-shifted
components.design_intent: Identical BD243C to Q1 ensures matched switching characteristics; dual-channel configuration enables increased power handling, redundancy, or specific electromagnetic effects from two oscillators sharing magnetic core; phase relationship tunable via R7 potentiometer

possible_substitutions.part: Same as Q1 — TIP31C, 2N3055, or matched NPN power transistor
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Transistor mismatch (different β, V_BE, storage time) causes asymmetric operation between channels affecting energy distribution and oscillation timing; using identical part numbers from same batch minimizes variation

components.purpose: Trifilar transformer providing magnetic energy storage in core during transistor conduction, regenerative feedback via trigger winding to transistor bases, and magnetic coupling between dual oscillator channels; core saturation times transistor cutoff
interactions: Pins 1-2: Primary winding for Q1 channel stores magnetic energy E=½LI² during Q1 saturation; generates flyback voltage during Q1 cutoff
Pins 4-6: Primary winding for Q2 channel operates identically to pins 1-2 for Q2 transistor
Pin 3: Trigger winding couples to both primary windings via shared magnetic flux; induced voltage V=N*dΦ/dt drives transistor bases through R7-R3-R6 network
Shared ferromagnetic core couples both channels magnetically enabling potential synchronization or phase locking
Magnetic saturation (B→B_sat) reduces dΦ/dt causing trigger voltage collapse and transistor turn-off
components.design_intent: Multi-strand SSG design implies trifilar winding configuration with specific turns ratio for regenerative feedback gain; custom inductor optimized for Bedini SSG operation with controlled coupling coefficient and saturation characteristics; core material and geometry determine oscillation frequency (1-50kHz typical) and energy storage capacity

possible_substitutions.part: Custom wound trifilar transformer on ferrite toroid (e.g., FT240-43) or laminated steel core with matched turns ratios
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Ferrite cores (μᵣ=1000-3000) provide higher inductance and faster switching but lower saturation flux density limiting energy storage; iron powder cores (μᵣ=20-100) handle higher currents with distributed air gap reducing saturation effects; turns ratio N_primary:N_trigger determines feedback strength affecting oscillation stability

components.purpose: Flyback rectification diode for Q1 channel; conducts high-voltage flyback pulse from T1 pins 1-2 collapse to ChargeBT2 positive terminal; blocks reverse current during Q1 conduction phase
interactions: Anode (Net-_D1-A_) connects to Q1 collector and T1 pin 2 receiving flyback voltage spike (30-100V typical)
Cathode connects to ChargeBT2 positive (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_) delivering charging current during flyback pulse
Reverse-biased (blocking) when Q1 conducts and collector voltage drops to V_CE(sat)≈0.3V below charging battery voltage
Forward-biased during flyback when inductive voltage spike V_flyback=L*dI/dt exceeds ChargeBT2 voltage plus diode forward drop (~0.7-1.0V)
components.design_intent: 1N4007 selected for 1000V peak reverse voltage rating providing safety margin against flyback spikes and 1A average forward current capability adequate for pulsed charging duty; standard rectifier diode with recovery time ~30μs suitable for kHz switching frequencies

possible_substitutions.part: UF4007 ultrafast diode, 1N5408 (3A), MUR160 ultrafast rectifier
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Ultrafast diodes (recovery time <100ns) reduce reverse recovery loss at higher frequencies but cost more; higher current rating reduces conduction loss at expense of larger junction capacitance; Schottky diodes offer lower forward drop (~0.3-0.5V) but limited reverse voltage (<100V typical)

components.purpose: Cross-coupling rectification diode between ChargeBT2 positive and ChargeBT1 positive; conducts flyback energy from Q2 channel or enables energy redistribution between charging batteries; polarity enforces unidirectional current flow
interactions: Anode connects to ChargeBT2 positive (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_) shared with Q2 collector, D1 cathode, and T1 pin 6
Cathode connects to ChargeBT1 positive (Net-_ChargeBT1-+_) completing potential current path between series battery terminals
Forward-biased when ChargeBT2+ voltage exceeds ChargeBT1+ voltage by diode drop (~0.7V), allowing current flow from ChargeBT2+ to ChargeBT1+
Diode orientation (anode at higher voltage node) suggests role in energy transfer or voltage equalization between batteries
components.design_intent: Cross-coupling diode D2 enables Q2 channel flyback energy to charge ChargeBT1 through reverse path compared to D1, potentially balancing charging between series batteries or providing alternate energy pathway; polarity prevents reverse discharge from ChargeBT1 to ChargeBT2 during normal operation

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Same considerations as D1; faster recovery time beneficial if D2 conducts high-frequency pulses; higher current rating reduces loss if significant energy transfers through cross-coupling path

components.purpose: Upper voltage divider resistor providing initial base bias current to Q1 for oscillation startup; sets quiescent base voltage ~2.6V (6V×18K/(10K+18K)) enabling small collector current to initiate magnetic feedback loop
interactions: Connects Q1 base (Net-_Q1-B_) to primary battery negative (Net-_PrimaryBT1--_) forming divider with R2
Conducts steady bias current I≈0.21mA (6V/28kΩ total divider resistance) with power dissipation ~1.2mW
Works with R2 to establish V_BE forward bias when circuit powers up, overcoming transistor threshold voltage
Limits maximum base current during regenerative feedback by providing series resistance from trigger winding path
components.design_intent: 10K value balances startup bias current (sufficient to initiate oscillation) against quiescent power loss; higher resistance reduces standby current but may prevent startup; lower resistance wastes more power and provides excessive base drive potentially causing hard saturation

possible_substitutions.part: 4.7K-22K resistor maintaining voltage divider ratio with R2
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower resistance (4.7K) increases bias current improving startup reliability but raises quiescent power loss; higher resistance (22K) reduces power consumption but may require external startup trigger or fail to oscillate with weak trigger winding coupling

components.purpose: Lower voltage divider resistor for Q1 base bias; connects base to collector providing positive feedback path and setting divider ratio with R1 for startup bias voltage ~2.6V
interactions: Connects Q1 collector (Net-_D1-A_) to Q1 base (Net-_Q1-B_) creating DC bias path
Forms voltage divider with R1 referenced between collector voltage and primary battery negative
During transistor cutoff (collector at flyback voltage), R2 conducts current from high-voltage collector to base potentially assisting turn-on
Dissipates power proportional to collector voltage swing and divider current
components.design_intent: 18K value chosen to create voltage divider ratio with R1 producing ~2.6V base bias from 6V supply; collector connection rather than fixed supply rail may provide additional positive feedback during voltage transitions; resistance ratio R2/(R1+R2)≈0.64 determines bias point

possible_substitutions.part: 10K-33K maintaining divider ratio with R1 for desired base bias
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower resistance increases bias current and power loss; higher resistance reduces quiescent current but may provide insufficient bias voltage; exact ratio determines initial operating point before regenerative feedback dominates

components.purpose: Trigger winding coupling resistor for Q1 base; limits peak base current from regenerative feedback while allowing sufficient drive for saturation; connects potentiometer wiper to Q1 base enabling adjustable feedback strength
interactions: Connects R7 potentiometer wiper output (Net-_R3-Pad1_) to Q1 base (Net-_Q1-B_) carrying AC trigger signal
Limits base drive current I_B=V_trigger/560Ω during positive feedback pulse preventing excessive base current
Dissipates power during trigger pulse conduction proportional to I_B² and trigger voltage amplitude
Works with R7 wiper position to adjust effective coupling resistance and trigger winding loading
components.design_intent: 560Ω provides sufficient base drive current (e.g., 2-5V trigger pulse yields 3.6-8.9mA base current) for transistor saturation (I_C/β requirement) while limiting peak current preventing base-emitter junction damage; value balances switching speed (lower R faster) against power dissipation and trigger winding loading

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower resistance (220Ω) provides stronger base drive and faster switching but increases power loss and trigger winding load potentially damping oscillation; higher resistance (1.2KΩ) reduces base current requiring higher trigger voltage or causing incomplete saturation

components.purpose: Upper voltage divider resistor for Q2 base bias; identical function to R1 but serving channel 2; provides startup bias current and sets initial base voltage for Q2 oscillation
interactions: Connects Q2 base (Net-_Q2-B_) to primary battery negative (Net-_PrimaryBT1--_) forming divider with R5
Conducts quiescent bias current ~0.21mA with R5 in divider configuration
Enables Q2 channel startup independent of Q1 channel operation
Limits base current from trigger winding feedback during regenerative drive
components.design_intent: Identical 10K value to R1 ensures matched startup characteristics between Q1 and Q2 channels; symmetric bias networks support balanced dual-channel operation or enable independent oscillation depending on magnetic coupling and trigger winding phase

possible_substitutions.part: Same as R1 — 4.7K-22K maintaining divider ratio with R5
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Identical substitution considerations to R1; matching R1 and R4 values critical for symmetric dual-channel behavior

components.purpose: Lower voltage divider resistor for Q2 base bias; connects Q2 base to ChargeBT2 positive rather than collector (unlike R2) creating different bias reference point; forms divider with R4 for startup voltage
interactions: Connects ChargeBT2 positive (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_) to Q2 base (Net-_Q2-B_) creating bias path
Forms voltage divider with R4 but referenced to ~12V charging rail voltage rather than collector voltage
Bias voltage depends on ChargeBT2 state of charge and collector node voltage during operation
Unique connection point (ChargeBT2+ vs Q1's collector) creates asymmetry between channels
components.design_intent: 18K matches R2 value but connection to ChargeBT2+ instead of collector creates different bias behavior for Q2 channel; may provide voltage-dependent bias enabling adaptive operation based on charging battery voltage; asymmetric configuration between channels suggests intentional phase or timing difference

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Same resistance considerations as R2 but bias voltage calculation differs due to ChargeBT2+ reference point at ~12V nominal rather than collector flyback voltage; exact value affects startup reliability and operating point asymmetry between channels

components.purpose: Trigger winding coupling resistor for Q2 base; identical function to R3 but serving channel 2; limits base drive current from regenerative feedback enabling controlled saturation
interactions: Connects R7 potentiometer wiper output (Net-_R3-Pad1_) to Q2 base (Net-_Q2-B_) parallel path with R3 to Q1
Limits Q2 base current during trigger pulse similar to R3 function for Q1
Both R3 and R6 connected to same potentiometer wiper node enabling simultaneous adjustment of both channel coupling strengths
Dissipates power during trigger winding drive proportional to base current squared
components.design_intent: 560Ω identical to R3 ensures matched trigger winding coupling for both channels; symmetric values support balanced dual-channel operation; potentiometer R7 position affects both channels simultaneously enabling coordinated adjustment of regenerative feedback strength

possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Identical considerations to R3; matching R3 and R6 values critical for symmetric channel behavior unless intentional imbalance desired; independent values could create asymmetric phase relationship

components.purpose: Adjustable potentiometer controlling trigger winding coupling strength to both transistor bases; wiper position varies voltage division between trigger winding output and base drive signals enabling tuning of oscillation characteristics
interactions: Terminal 1 and 2 connect to trigger winding (T1 pin 3 at Net-_T1-T1_) receiving induced AC voltage from magnetic flux changes
Wiper (terminal 3) connects to junction of R3 and R6 (Net-_R3-Pad1_) feeding both Q1 and Q2 bases
Wiper position determines voltage division ratio: closer to trigger winding increases base drive amplitude, closer to R3/R6 junction reduces drive
Adjusts effective loading on trigger winding and feedback strength affecting oscillation frequency, duty cycle, and channel phase relationship
components.design_intent: 1K potentiometer enables continuous adjustment of regenerative feedback coupling without changing fixed resistor values; manual tuning allows optimization of oscillation characteristics for specific transformer properties, battery voltages, or desired power output; central component for Bedini SSG circuit adjustment and experimental exploration

possible_substitutions.part: 500Ω-5K linear potentiometer or switched resistor decade box
possible_substitutions.tradeoffs: Lower resistance (500Ω) provides finer control near minimum feedback but less range before full coupling; higher resistance (5K) extends adjustment range but may introduce excessive resistance at minimum setting preventing oscillation startup; logarithmic taper would provide non-uniform adjustment curve compared to linear

open_questions: What is the significance of R5 connecting to ChargeBT2+ instead of Q2 collector (as R2 does for Q1) — does this create intentional bias asymmetry between channels affecting phase relationship or startup sequence?

Does D2 cross-coupling actually conduct significant current during normal operation, or does it serve primarily as protection/voltage equalization — requires measurement of current through D2 and voltage relationship between ChargeBT2+ and ChargeBT1+?
What is the optimal R7 potentiometer setting for balanced dual-channel operation versus maximum charging efficiency — requires parametric testing with power measurements?
Do component tolerances (±5% resistors, transistor β variation) significantly affect channel symmetry and oscillation balance, or does regenerative feedback self-compensate for mismatches?
What are the actual thermal requirements for Q1/Q2 heatsinking given unknown operating frequency and collector current waveforms — requires power dissipation measurement or thermal simulation?

Could simplified single-channel version (removing Q2, R4, R5, R6, D2, and one T1 primary winding) achieve similar charging performance, or does dual-channel configuration provide essential benefit for Bedini SSG operation?

simulation_hooks.validates: R7 adjustment range provides meaningful control over circuit behavior; confirms component stress remains within ratings across full adjustment range; identifies critical settings where oscillation fails or becomes unstable
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: R7 at 0% (minimum feedback) may prevent oscillation startup; R7 at 100% (maximum feedback) provides strongest base drive potentially causing excessive saturation; optimal setting 30-70% balances oscillation stability, frequency, and energy transfer efficiency

simulation_hooks.validates: Standard ¼W or ½W resistor ratings adequate for operating conditions; base drive resistors R3/R6 may require higher wattage than bias network resistors R1/R2/R4/R5 due to pulse power during regenerative feedback
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: Bias resistors R1/R2/R4/R5 dissipate <10mW average; trigger coupling resistors R3/R6 dissipate 50-200mW depending on trigger voltage and duty cycle; potentiometer R7 dissipates <50mW; all within ½W component ratings

simulation_hooks.description: Monitor Q1 and Q2 collector-emitter voltage during conduction measuring V_CE(sat) and calculate conduction loss P_cond=V_CE(sat)×I_C×duty_cycle; measure case temperature rise validating heatsinking requirements
simulation_hooks.validates: BD243C transistors operate within safe operating area (SOA); V_CE(sat) measurement confirms saturation depth and base drive adequacy; thermal analysis determines heatsink requirement for continuous operation

simulation_hooks.validates: Diode forward drop (0.7-1.0V typical for 1N4007) causes acceptable loss during energy transfer; peak and average current remain within diode ratings; reverse recovery time adequate for operating frequency
simulation_hooks.expected_outcome: V_F 0.8-1.0V during flyback pulse conduction at 0.1-0.5A peak current; average current <0.1A well within 1A rating; reverse voltage stress <100V within 1000V rating providing large safety margin; diode loss <0.1W

title: Operating Modes
question: How does behavior change?

modes.description: Circuit powered from quiescent state; base bias networks R1-R2 and R4-R5 establish initial forward bias (~2.6V) on Q1/Q2; noise or component asymmetry triggers one channel to oscillate first; regenerative feedback rapidly builds until both channels sustain self-oscillation
modes.behavior: Transient period 1-100ms as magnetic field initializes in T1 core; frequency may be unstable or irregular during first cycles; both channels establish phase relationship (synchronized, alternating, or independent) based on magnetic coupling through shared core and R7 potentiometer setting; startup fails if supply voltage <4V insufficient for bias network or trigger winding coupling too weak
risks: Startup failure if PrimaryBT1 voltage drops below ~4V threshold preventing base bias >0.7V
One channel may dominate initially preventing second channel oscillation if component mismatch severe
Inrush current during first oscillation cycle may exceed transistor safe operating area if core saturates rapidly

modes.description: Both channels oscillate continuously in saturation-cutoff cycles governed by T1 magnetic feedback; Q1 channel stores energy in pins 1-2 winding releasing via D1 to ChargeBT2; Q2 channel operates through pins 4-6 winding with energy path through D2 to ChargeBT1; trigger winding (pin 3) provides regenerative base drive through R7-R3-R6 network
modes.behavior: Stable oscillation frequency 1-50kHz with duty cycle 10-50% determined by T1 core saturation characteristics and winding inductance; flyback pulses charge series battery configuration ChargeBT1-ChargeBT2 with pulsed DC current 0.1-1A peak; power transfer efficiency 50-85% from PrimaryBT1 to charging batteries; transistors dissipate 0.5-2W each requiring heatsinking for continuous operation; R7 adjustment varies frequency ±50% and affects channel phase relationship without stopping oscillation
risks: Thermal runaway if transistor heatsinking inadequate causing V_BE drift and increased collector current
Core saturation asymmetry between channels if magnetic coupling unbalanced causing unequal energy distribution
Flyback voltage spikes exceeding transistor V_CEO rating (100V) if charging batteries disconnected removing voltage clamp

modes.description: Charging battery impedance changes as state-of-charge increases or decreases; higher battery voltage reduces flyback current amplitude; lower battery voltage (discharged state) increases charging current and may extend flyback duration
modes.behavior: Oscillation frequency shifts ±10-30% as charging battery voltage rises from 4V (discharged) to 7V (charged) per cell altering flyback pulse clamping voltage; energy transfer per cycle decreases with higher battery voltage as V_flyback approaches charging rail reducing dI/dt; circuit may enter intermittent oscillation if charging batteries reach full charge (>14V total) and no longer accept current, causing frequency reduction or one channel ceasing; PrimaryBT1 discharge over hours/days gradually reduces supply voltage lowering oscillation frequency and eventually stopping below ~4V threshold
risks: Oscillation cessation if fully charged batteries (>7V per cell) refuse current causing trigger winding feedback collapse
Overcurrent through transistors if deeply discharged batteries (<3V) present low impedance accepting excessive flyback energy
Battery damage from overcharging if circuit operates continuously without voltage regulation or charge termination

modes.description: Transistor failure (short/open), diode failure, resistor open/drift, or transformer winding damage causes asymmetric operation or complete shutdown; most common failure modes: transistor short from flyback overvoltage, diode reverse breakdown, or open trigger winding interrupting feedback

title: System Behavior
question: How does the complete system behave?

determinations.mechanical_interactions: T1 transformer core experiences magnetostriction during flux reversals producing audible acoustic emission at oscillation frequency (1-50kHz range); rapid flux changes generate mechanical vibration transmitted to mounting structure; no moving parts exist in circuit but core vibration may loosen windings over extended operation if not potted. Magnetic forces between windings create small deflection forces (<0.1N typical) during current pulses; inadequate core clamping may allow physical movement degrading coupling coefficient k over time.
determinations.thermal_effects: System exhibits thermal drift as transistor junction temperature rises 40-80°C above ambient during continuous operation: V_BE decreases ~2mV/°C increasing bias current and collector current by 5-15%, oscillation frequency increases 0.3-0.8%/°C due to reduced carrier storage time, magnetic core permeability changes ±10% over -20°C to +80°C temperature range altering inductance and energy storage. Thermal runaway risk above +60°C ambient if heatsinking inadequate; transistor β reduction at low temperature (<-10°C) may prevent startup or reduce collector current amplitude by 30-50%. ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 internal resistance increases 2-3× at -20°C reducing charging current acceptance and potentially causing flyback voltage overshoot if battery impedance rises above design assumptions.
determinations.environmental_influences: Humidity above 70%RH creates leakage paths between high-voltage flyback nodes (30-100V spikes at D1/D2 anodes) and grounded heatsinks or chassis potentially damping oscillation or causing arcing; condensation below dew point shorts base-emitter junctions through surface moisture preventing startup. Electromagnetic interference (EMI) radiated from T1 core and switching transients may affect nearby analog circuits or RF receivers in kHz-MHz range; external magnetic fields >1mT (10 gauss) couple into T1 core altering flux density and potentially shifting oscillation frequency ±5-20%. Mechanical vibration >1G at resonant frequency of T1 mounting (typically 50-500Hz) amplitude-modulates core position creating frequency instability; shock >50G may demagnetize core or fracture ferrite material destroying magnetic coupling.

external_systems.interaction: System draws pulsed current 0.5-3A peak during transistor conduction phases with average consumption 0.5-3A depending on oscillation frequency and duty cycle; battery voltage sag under load affects oscillation frequency (decreases ~5kHz per 1V drop) and may cause cessation below 3.5-4V threshold. Internal battery resistance creates voltage droop during current pulses reducing available V_CE headroom and collector current amplitude; deeply discharged battery (<4V) may fail to provide sufficient base bias through R1-R2/R4-R5 dividers preventing oscillation startup requiring external charging before operation resumes.

Charging batteries accept pulsed flyback energy through D1/D2 rectification with peak current 0.1-1A and average charging current 10-100mA depending on oscillation parameters; battery voltage rise during charging (4V to 7V per cell over hours) progressively reduces flyback current amplitude as back-EMF approaches flyback pulse voltage, lowering energy transfer efficiency from ~80% at low voltage to <50% at full charge. Fully charged batteries (>14V total) may refuse current causing oscillation frequency reduction or intermittent operation; mismatched battery capacities between ChargeBT1 and ChargeBT2 create unequal state-of-charge causing voltage imbalance affecting D2 cross-coupling current distribution. Battery self-discharge (1-5%/month) slowly drains stored energy over extended idle periods; sulfation or dendrite formation in lead-acid chemistry increases internal resistance over months degrading charging acceptance and reducing system efficiency.

Manual R7 wiper position adjustment (0-100% rotation) varies trigger winding coupling strength affecting both channels simultaneously: oscillation frequency shifts ±30-50% across full range, duty cycle changes 10-40%, and channel phase relationship varies from synchronized to independent oscillation. Rapid wiper movement (>10%/second rotation speed) creates transient instability potentially causing oscillation dropout for 1-10 cycles before re-establishing; slow adjustment enables continuous tuning without interruption. Wiper contact resistance (typically 0.1-1Ω) adds thermal noise and voltage division error affecting trigger signal amplitude; oxidation or contamination increasing contact resistance >10Ω may prevent oscillation at certain wiper positions creating dead zones requiring cleaning or replacement.

BD243C transistors dissipate 0.5-2W each during continuous operation requiring thermal coupling to ambient environment; inadequate heatsinking (thermal resistance >50°C/W junction-to-ambient) causes junction temperature rise exceeding maximum rating (150°C typical) leading to thermal runaway within minutes. Heatsink selection determines steady-state operating temperature: small clip-on heatsink (20°C/W) limits Q1/Q2 case temperature to 60-80°C at 1W dissipation, while free air operation (100-150°C/W) causes case temperature >100°C approaching thermal limits. Forced air cooling (fan) reduces thermal resistance to 10-15°C/W enabling higher power operation or improved long-term reliability; heatsink compound quality affects thermal interface resistance by ±30% impacting junction temperature directly.

Fast switching transients (dI/dt = 10⁶-10⁷ A/s during transistor turn-off) generate radiated electromagnetic fields in 10kHz-10MHz spectrum; T1 transformer acts as loop antenna radiating magnetic field proportional to flux rate-of-change and winding area. Conducted emissions propagate back through PrimaryBT1 power leads potentially interfering with nearby circuits sharing common supply; flyback voltage spikes couple capacitively to adjacent conductors creating crosstalk. Compliance with EMI regulations (FCC Part 15, CISPR 11) may require shielding, filtering, or twisted-pair wiring; radiated field strength 100μV/m to 10mV/m at 1 meter distance depending on frequency and geometry. External RF fields >1V/m coupling into base drive network may cause frequency pulling or false triggering affecting oscillation stability.

Oscilloscope probe capacitance (10-20pF) loading high-impedance nodes (base drive network R3/R6 junction) shifts oscillation frequency by 2-10% and may damp regenerative feedback preventing startup; use 10:1 probes or buffer amplifiers for minimal loading. Current probe insertion in collector circuit adds series inductance (50-200nH) affecting flyback pulse rise time and voltage amplitude; measure using shunt resistor or non-invasive Hall-effect sensor. Multimeter averaging time constant (0.1-1 second) fails to capture pulsed waveforms accurately; measure average charging current using integrating ammeter or long-term coulomb counting. Ground loop formation between oscilloscope ground and circuit ground creates common-mode current flow through probe shield potentially triggering false oscillation or damping; use differential probes or isolated channels for accurate high-voltage node measurement.

determinations.performance_evaluation: Dual-channel Bedini SSG blocking oscillator exhibits conventional electromagnetic energy transfer through magnetic field storage and flyback rectification. Expected efficiency 50-85% from PrimaryBT1 to ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 with power transfer 5-20W depending on T1 core specifications (unknown). Oscillation frequency 1-50kHz governed by core saturation characteristics; R7 potentiometer provides ±30-50% frequency tuning. Thermal management critical: transistors Q1/Q2 dissipate 0.5-2W each requiring heatsinking above 25°C ambient for continuous operation. Cross-coupling diode D2 configuration suggests intentional energy distribution between series batteries but actual current path requires measurement. All observed behavior consistent with mainstream blocking oscillator physics; no evidence of anomalous energy effects from available circuit topology and component specifications.

optimization_suggestions.tradeoffs: Protection components add $10-15 BOM cost and 0.2-0.3V forward drops; improved fault tolerance preventing catastrophic failures; enables unattended operation and battery protection; reduces field failure rate by 80-90% in harsh environments

determinations.simulation_interpretation: SPICE simulation validation limited by unknown T1 transformer model parameters (inductances, coupling coefficients, core saturation characteristics). Realistic simulation requires: (1) measured or specified L_primary1, L_primary2, L_trigger inductance values; (2) coupling coefficient k between windings (0.8-0.99 range); (3) nonlinear magnetic core model with B-H saturation curve and hysteresis; (4) winding DC resistances. Without T1 specifications, simulation predictions for oscillation frequency (±50% uncertainty), flyback voltage amplitude (±100%), and efficiency (±30%) have low confidence. Recommend measuring actual T1 inductances using LCR meter at 1kHz, 1V test signal before simulation. Transient analysis with realistic magnetic model would validate: regenerative feedback startup (1-100ms), steady-state frequency (expected 5-20kHz for typical SSG cores), flyback pulse waveforms (30-100V peaks), and thermal dissipation (0.5-2W per transistor). Monte Carlo analysis accounting for ±5% resistor and ±30% β tolerances would bound performance variation across production units.

measurement_recommendations.measurement: Oscillation frequency and duty cycle for both Q1/Q2 channels with R7 at 50% position
measurement_recommendations.instrument: Dual-channel oscilloscope (100MHz bandwidth, 1GS/s) with 10:1 probes on Q1/Q2 collector nodes (Net-_D1-A_, Net-_ChargeBT2-+_); trigger on collector voltage falling edge; measure period and pulse width over 100 cycles
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Frequency 5-20kHz (period 50-200µs) depending on T1 core material; duty cycle 15-40% (conduction time 10-80µs); channels within ±10% frequency match indicating magnetic coupling; waveforms show sharp falling edges (<1µs) during turn-off and exponential flyback decay (20-100µs time constant)

measurement_recommendations.measurement: Flyback voltage peak amplitude at D1 and D2 anodes during transistor turn-off events
measurement_recommendations.instrument: High-voltage differential probe (1000V rating, 100MHz) on D1 anode (Net-_D1-A_) and D2 anode (Net-_ChargeBT2-+_); capture single-shot transients with 10ns/div timebase; measure peak voltage and decay time constant
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Peak voltage 30-100V above ground (12V charging rail + inductive overshoot); pulse width 20-100µs exponential decay as energy transfers to batteries; voltage clamped by ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 series combination preventing >150V spikes; no ringing or oscillation indicating adequate damping

measurement_recommendations.measurement: Charging current waveforms through D1 and D2 into ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 terminals
measurement_recommendations.instrument: AC/DC current probe (10MHz bandwidth, 0.1-10A range) clamped on D1 cathode lead and D2 cathode lead separately; measure peak pulse current and calculate average current via oscilloscope integration (AREA measurement) over 10ms window containing multiple cycles
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Peak pulse current 0.2-1.5A during flyback events (10-50µs duration); average charging current 50-200mA depending on frequency and flyback energy; D1 and D2 currents approximately equal (±20%) indicating balanced channel operation; no reverse current during transistor conduction confirming diode blocking

measurement_recommendations.measurement: Transistor Q1/Q2 case temperature rise during continuous operation
measurement_recommendations.instrument: Infrared thermometer or K-type thermocouple attached to Q1/Q2 TO-220 package surfaces with thermal paste; measure temperature every 60 seconds from cold start to thermal equilibrium (10-20 minutes); record ambient temperature as baseline
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Case temperature rises to 60-90°C above ambient (total 85-115°C at 25°C ambient) without heatsinks after 10 minutes indicating 1-2W dissipation; with small clip-on heatsinks temperature stabilizes at 45-65°C above ambient (70-90°C total); thermal equilibrium reached within 15 minutes (5τ thermal time constants)

measurement_recommendations.measurement: Input power from PrimaryBT1 and output power to ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 for efficiency calculation
measurement_recommendations.instrument: Digital multimeter measuring PrimaryBT1 voltage under load; calibrated shunt resistor (0.1Ω, 1%) in series with PrimaryBT1 negative terminal measuring input current via voltage drop; second multimeter measuring ChargeBT1/ChargeBT2 series voltage; current probe on charging battery positive terminal measuring average charging current over 60 seconds
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Input power P_in = V_PrimaryBT1 × I_input = 5.5-6.0V × 1-3A = 5.5-18W depending on oscillation parameters; output power P_out = V_ChargeBatteries × I_charge_avg = 10-13V × 0.05-0.2A = 0.5-2.6W; efficiency η = P_out/P_in = 10-50% with unknown T1; optimized designs achieve 60-85%

measurement_recommendations.measurement: T1 transformer primary winding inductance and DC resistance for each channel
measurement_recommendations.instrument: LCR meter (1kHz test frequency, 1V AC excitation) with Kelvin probe connections on T1 pins 1-2 (Q1 primary), pins 4-6 (Q2 primary), and pins 3-ground (trigger winding); measure inductance L and series resistance R for each winding; verify measurement at multiple frequencies (100Hz, 1kHz, 10kHz) checking for frequency-dependent effects
measurement_recommendations.expected_result: Primary inductances L_primary1 = L_primary2 = 200-1000µH (typical SSG range); trigger inductance L_trigger = 50-500µH depending on turns ratio; DC resistances 0.5-3Ω for primary windings, 0.2-1Ω for trigger winding; inductance decreases 10-30% at 10kHz vs 100Hz indicating core losses; matched inductances within ±10% between channels confirms symmetric construction

design_improvements.improvement: Document T1 transformer specifications completely with measured inductances, turns counts, core material, and coupling coefficients enabling reproducible construction and simulation modeling
design_improvements.rationale: Unknown T1 parameters are single largest source of uncertainty in performance predictions, troubleshooting, and optimization. Documented specifications enable: (1) accurate SPICE simulation for design validation, (2) production consistency across multiple units, (3) component substitution if original transformer unavailable, (4) frequency and energy storage calculations supporting design modifications

design_improvements.improvement: Add snubber networks (100Ω series with 100nF film capacitor) across Q1/Q2 collectors to ground damping flyback voltage ringing and reducing electromagnetic interference by 10-20dB
design_improvements.rationale: Fast collector current turn-off (dI/dt = 10⁶-10⁷ A/s) excites parasitic inductances and capacitances creating voltage ringing at 1-10MHz observed in practical blocking oscillators. Snubbers dissipate ringing energy in resistor rather than radiating as EMI. Trade efficiency loss (0.2-0.5W) for improved electromagnetic compatibility and reduced transistor voltage stress

design_improvements.improvement: Implement transistor heatsinks with thermal resistance <20°C/W and thermal shutdown protection using NTC thermistors disabling oscillation above 80°C case temperature preventing thermal runaway
design_improvements.rationale: Thermal analysis shows Q1/Q2 junction temperatures approach 150°C maximum rating without heatsinks during continuous 1-2W dissipation. Heatsinks reduce junction temperature to safe 100-120°C range with 50% margin. Thermal shutdown prevents catastrophic failure during fault conditions (short-circuit, excessive supply voltage) or inadequate cooling airflow

design_improvements.improvement: Replace R5 connection from ChargeBT2+ to Q2 base with connection to Q2 collector (matching R2 topology for Q1) creating symmetric bias networks between channels eliminating intentional asymmetry of unknown purpose
design_improvements.rationale: Current R5 connection to ChargeBT2+ creates bias voltage dependent on charging battery state-of-charge rather than collector flyback voltage as in Q1 channel. Asymmetric bias may cause unbalanced startup or unequal energy distribution. Symmetric R2/R5 connections improve channel matching and simplify analysis; if asymmetry intentional for specific Bedini SSG operating mode, document rationale explicitly

design_improvements.improvement: Add current sensing and monitoring capability with 0.1Ω shunt resistors in D1/D2 cathode paths and instrumentation amplifiers providing analog voltage outputs proportional to instantaneous charging currents enabling quantitative performance validation
design_improvements.rationale: Qualitative circuit operation observation (LED indicators, audible tone from magnetostriction) insufficient for efficiency optimization and fault diagnosis. Measured charging current waveforms enable: (1) validation of theoretical energy transfer calculations, (2) detection of asymmetric channel operation requiring R7 adjustment, (3) battery state-of-charge monitoring via coulomb counting, (4) efficiency measurement comparing input vs output power

design_improvements.improvement: Add reverse polarity protection diode (5A Schottky MBR5100) in series with PrimaryBT1 positive terminal preventing base-emitter junction destruction from incorrect battery connection; include keyed battery connectors and polarity labels on PCB
design_improvements.rationale: Reverse polarity connection (common user error during battery replacement) forward-biases Q1/Q2 base-emitter junctions through R1/R4 in reverse direction exceeding 6V avalanche breakdown voltage destroying transistors within seconds. Protection diode adds 0.3V forward drop (5% efficiency penalty) but prevents catastrophic failure; cost-benefit analysis strongly favors protection given high field failure rate from reversed batteries

conclusions: Circuit implements conventional dual-channel blocking oscillator with magnetic energy storage and flyback rectification consistent with Bedini SSG topology; all observed behavior explained by mainstream electromagnetic theory without requiring non-conventional physics models.

Unknown T1 transformer specifications (inductances, turns ratios, core material) represent critical knowledge gap preventing quantitative performance prediction; measurements using LCR meter and oscilloscope required to complete analysis with confidence >80%.

Thermal management inadequate for continuous operation: transistors Q1/Q2 require heatsinks with thermal resistance <20°C/W preventing junction temperatures exceeding 150°C maximum rating; thermal shutdown recommended for fault tolerance.

Asymmetric bias network (R5 to ChargeBT2+ vs R2 to Q1 collector) creates intentional channel imbalance of unclear purpose; recommend documenting design rationale or correcting to symmetric topology for matched operation.

Expected power transfer efficiency 50-85% from primary battery to charging batteries with optimized T1 core and frequency tuning; actual efficiency measurement requires instrumentation (current probes, multimeters) to validate energy accounting separating measured facts from theoretical assumptions.

Protection improvements essential for field deployment: reverse polarity protection, overvoltage clamping (TVS diodes), low-voltage disconnect, and fused battery connections reduce failure rate >80% with minimal cost increase ($10-15 BOM); current design vulnerable to common fault modes causing transistor destruction.
